intent: I'm writing the discussion section of a paper on the cosmic-ray positron excess and I need to lay out, line of evidence by line of evidence, whether the excess actually requires dark-matter annihilation or whether nearby pulsars plus solar-modulation systematics can absorb it. Specifically: what spectral features did PAMELA and AMS-02 actually measure, what does the HAWC pulsar evidence say, what do the AMS-02 antiprotons do to the heavy-DM hypothesis, and how much of the low-energy structure is really just charge-sign-dependent solar modulation rather than a primary source? Where do these explanations genuinely conflict?
nuggets: PAMELA (Adriani2009) discovered that the positron fraction RISES with energy above ~10 GeV (1.5-100 GeV range), contradicting the smooth fall predicted by pure secondary production (Moskalenko & Strong), and explicitly framed the rise as requiring either dark-matter annihilation or nearby pulsars, while noting none of the published models fit the data well.

AMS-02 (Aguilar2021) sharpened the positron excess into a quantitative spectral signature: an onset at 25.2 +/- 1.8 GeV, a maximum near ~290 GeV, and a finite source-term exponential cutoff energy E_s = 810 (+310/-180) GeV established at more than 4 sigma (4.07 sigma) significance.

Hooper2017 argues that HAWC (plus Milagro) TeV gamma-ray observations of Geminga and B0656+14 show these nearby pulsars inject enough high-energy e+e- that pulsars INVARIABLY produce a positron flux similar in spectrum and magnitude to the PAMELA/AMS-02 excess, making them the likely dominant source.

Cuoco2017 shows that the AMS-02 ANTIPROTON spectrum is fit well by purely secondary antiprotons (no primary/DM component required) and sets robust limits that strongly disfavor thermal heavy DM (e.g. the ~2.8 TeV thermal wino) - so a DM explanation of the positron excess must avoid overproducing antiprotons.

The DM-vs-pulsar debate hinges on whether the same source must show up in antiprotons: leptophilic/pulsar explanations evade the antiproton constraint, whereas generic WIMP annihilation into quarks/gauge bosons is squeezed by Cuoco2017's antiproton limits, a tension the positron data alone (Aguilar2021, Adriani2009) cannot resolve.

Potgieter2021 demonstrates that a large part of the LOW-energy positron behavior is charge-sign-dependent solar (drift) modulation tied to the 22-year heliospheric polarity cycle - significant below a few GeV - and that the simple force-field approximation used by AMS-02 is inadequate for antimatter, meaning sub-GeV structure is a modulation systematic rather than a primary-source signal.

The lines of evidence conflict on locality and on antiprotons: PAMELA/AMS-02 establish the excess but cannot identify the source; Hooper2017 attributes it to nearby pulsars; Cuoco2017 uses antiprotons to disfavor heavy DM; and Potgieter2021 warns that the low-energy end is contaminated by modulation systematics - so the excess does NOT uniquely require dark matter.
rationale: Read in full: Adriani2009, Aguilar2021, Hooper2017, Potgieter2021; read full conclusion + methods/results of Cuoco2017. Nugget 1 = Adriani2009 abstract, 'HIGH ENERGY ANOMALY' section and conclusions, Table I. Nugget 2 = Aguilar2021 abstract and section 1 (E_s=810 GeV excluded at 4.07 sigma). Nugget 3 = Hooper2017 abstract, introduction, conclusions. Nugget 4 = Cuoco2017 section 2.1 (secondary antiprotons fit well, not required) and section 4 conclusion (strongly disfavor thermal wino regardless of DM profile). Nugget 5 synthesizes Cuoco2017's quark/gauge-boson limits against positron-only inference of Aguilar2021/Adriani2009. Nugget 6 = Potgieter2021 abstract, section 1 (force-field inadequate, misleading), section 9; charge-sign point corroborated in Adriani2009. Nugget 7 = synthesis across the four directly-answering papers plus modulation caveat. Off: Abdollahi2017 and Aguilar2019 are about the electron side / combined spectrum, off-target for the positron-excess origin debate.

intent: I'm trying to understand the leptonic spectral asymmetry that the dark-matter-vs-pulsar interpretations have to explain. Why do AMS-02 see a sharp cutoff in the positron flux but none in the electron flux, and how does that square with the Fermi-LAT combined electron-plus-positron spectrum and the original PAMELA positron-fraction rise? I specifically want the measured numbers - onset energies, cutoff energies and their significances, spectral indices - across the experiments, and I want to know what this positron/electron asymmetry implies for whether a single dark-matter source can produce equal electrons and positrons or whether separate (e.g. pulsar) sources are required.
nuggets: AMS-02 (Aguilar2021) measure a positron flux with a finite exponential source-term cutoff at E_s = 810 (+310/-180) GeV (>4 sigma), whereas AMS-02 (Aguilar2019) find the ELECTRON flux has NO exponential cutoff below 1.9 TeV at the 5 sigma level - a direct positron/electron asymmetry.

The positron excess onset (25.2 +/- 1.8 GeV, Aguilar2021) and the electron excess onset (42.1 +5.4/-5.2 GeV, Aguilar2019) occur at different energies and the AMS Collaboration explicitly states the electron excess is of a DIFFERENT NATURE from the positron excess, evidence that most high-energy electrons come from different sources than high-energy positrons.

Aguilar2019 tested whether a dark-matter-like source term identical to the positron source term exists in the electrons and found the electron data are consistent BOTH with the presence and with the absence of such a term - so the electron spectrum alone cannot confirm or exclude a common DM source.

Fermi-LAT (Abdollahi2017) measured the combined electron+positron spectrum from 7 GeV to 2 TeV, fit it as a broken power law with a break near 50 GeV and an index of 3.07 +/- 0.02 above the break, and EXCLUDED an exponential cutoff below 1.8 TeV at 95% CL - consistent with the no-cutoff electron behavior but in tension with the 810 GeV positron cutoff being a feature of the total lepton flux.

PAMELA (Adriani2009) originally established the anomaly as a RISING positron FRACTION above ~10 GeV (a ratio), which the later AMS-02 flux measurements (Aguilar2021/Aguilar2019) resolved into separately-shaped positron and electron FLUXES - clarifying that the rising fraction is driven by the distinct positron component.

Hooper2017's pulsar model naturally predicts a positron spectrum with an energy-loss feature around 400-500 GeV (e.g. ~476 GeV for Geminga's ~370,000-year age) and a cutoff, providing an astrophysical explanation for the positron flux drop-off without invoking an electron cutoff at the same energy - matching the observed positron/electron asymmetry.

The combined picture forces a choice: a generic DM source producing equal e+ and e- is hard to reconcile with the asymmetry (cutoff in positrons but not electrons), favoring source classes like pulsars that inject e+e- with a positron-side spectral feature, while DM is not excluded because the electron data are agnostic (Aguilar2019).
rationale: Read in full: Aguilar2021, Aguilar2019, Adriani2009, Hooper2017; read Abdollahi2017 results in full. Nugget 1 = Aguilar2021 (positron cutoff 810 GeV >4 sigma) and Aguilar2019 (electron no cutoff below 1.9 TeV at 5 sigma). Nugget 2 = Aguilar2019 abstract (onset 42.1 GeV, 'different nature') and Aguilar2021 (positron onset 25.2 GeV). Nugget 3 = Aguilar2019 (electron data consistent both with and without an identical source term). Nugget 4 = Abdollahi2017 abstract and section VII (break ~50 GeV, index 3.07, exclude cutoff below 1.8 TeV 95% CL). Nugget 5 = Adriani2009 positron-fraction sections contrasted with AMS flux measurements (why Adriani2009 is context). Nugget 6 = Hooper2017 (feature 400-500 GeV, 476 GeV for Geminga 370 kyr). Nugget 7 = synthesis tying Aguilar2019's agnosticism to Hooper2017's positron feature and the measured asymmetry. Off: Cuoco2017 (antiprotons) and Potgieter2021 (modulation) are other observables, mis-retrievals for the e+/e- spectral-shape question. All numbers verbatim from read text.

intent: I'm trying to adjudicate the central debate over the sub-TeV cosmic-ray proton/nuclei spectral hardening: is the ~200-400 GV break an intrinsic source/injection effect, a Galactic propagation (diffusion-coefficient) effect, or partly an artifact of stitching together experiments whose absolute energy scales disagree? I want each camp's actual evidence laid side by side - the specific break rigidities different experiments report, the argument that ties the break to propagation rather than injection, and the explicit treatment of inter-experiment energy-scale offsets - so I can see which interpretation each paper's data actually supports.
nuggets: PAMELA (Adriani2011) directly observes a hardening in the proton spectrum at a break rigidity of 232 (+35/-30) GV, where the spectral index changes from ~2.85 (80-232 GV) to ~2.67 (>232 GV), with helium hardening at a similar rigidity (~243 GV).

AMS-02 places the proton hardening at a higher rigidity (~336 GV) than PAMELA's ~232 GV, and Lipari2019's global fit across PAMELA/AMS-02/calorimeters centers the hardening near ~650 GeV with a larger spectral-index step than the magnetic spectrometers alone indicate.

Schroer2021 argues the break at ~300 GV must be a propagation effect - a break in the Galactic diffusion coefficient (Rb ~290-300 GV in their D(R)) - NOT an injection/source effect, because the same break appears in secondary-to-primary ratios, which would not happen if the feature originated at the accelerators.

Adriani2011 (PAMELA) frames the hardening instead as a possible source effect, comparing to multi-source models (e.g. Zatsepin-Sokolskaya with novae/superbubble sources) and stating the data challenge the standard single-population SNR-acceleration-plus-diffusive-propagation paradigm (GALPROP does not reproduce the data).

The apparent disagreement in break rigidity and spectral indices between experiments is in large part a cross-calibration problem: Dembinski2017 shows each experiment's energy scale carries a ~10-20% systematic uncertainty that, for a spectral index ~2.7, produces ~18% apparent flux shifts, and derives explicit energy-scale offset/adjustment factors from a global fit.

Lipari2019 attributes the systematically softer slope above the break seen by AMS-02 (alpha2 ~2.72) versus the calorimeters (alpha2 ~2.44-2.62) to AMS-02's limited maximum rigidity (~1.2-1.8 TV) not capturing the full development of the hardening - i.e. a measurement-range/energy-scale effect, not a real spectral disagreement.

Lipari2019 explicitly enumerates that post-PAMELA models attribute the hardening to EITHER acceleration (two accelerator classes / two acceleration regimes) OR propagation (rigidity-dependent diffusion changing regime), leaving the source-vs-propagation question open.
rationale: Read in full: Adriani2011, Lipari2019, Schroer2021, Dembinski2017; Maurin2019 read in full but is the USINE propagation-code tool paper, does not adjudicate the break, so off. Nugget 1 = Adriani2011 (proton hardening 232 GV, 2.85->2.67; helium 243 GV). Nugget 2 = Lipari2019 Table 1 (AMS-02 break ~336 GV vs PAMELA 232 GV; combined Eb ~650 GeV). Nugget 3 = Schroer2021 Intro/section II (break ~300 GV must be transport not injection; appears in secondary/primary; Rb ~290-300 GV). Nugget 4 = Adriani2011 (Zatsepin-Sokolskaya multi-source, challenge paradigm, GALPROP fails). Nugget 5 = Dembinski2017 section 2 (10% offset -> 18% flux for alpha=2.7; 10-20% energy-scale uncertainty; GSF offsets). Nugget 6 = Lipari2019 (AMS-02 alpha2 ~2.716 vs calorimeters 2.44-2.62, attributed to max rigidity). Nugget 7 = Lipari2019 section 4 (acceleration-vs-propagation enumeration). Discrimination: source-claim, propagation-claim, energy-scale-artifact, and cross-experiment framing are in four different papers.

intent: I want to test how 'universal' the cosmic-ray spectral features really are across species and across the energy decades, and where the universality breaks down. Specifically: do protons, helium, and heavier nuclei share a common rigidity-dependent hardening/softening shape, or do they require different source spectra? Where does a single self-consistent transport model succeed, and what are the documented anomalies (the proton/helium index difference, the iron low-rigidity anomaly, the second softening, and the PeV-region experimental disagreements) that no single picture cleanly explains?
nuggets: PAMELA (Adriani2011) finds proton and helium have DIFFERENT spectral shapes/indices - the proton index (~2.82, 30-1000 GV) is steeper than helium (~2.73), a robust difference of Delta-gamma = gamma_p - gamma_He ~= 0.101 - already breaking the assumption of a single universal source spectrum for all species.

Schroer2021 independently concludes that protons, helium, and heavier nuclei require slightly DIFFERENT injection (source) spectra - H softer by ~0.05, He harder by ~0.02 relative to heavier nuclei - which is at odds with rigidity-only diffusive shock acceleration and corroborates the PAMELA p/He difference.

The hardening (and the higher-energy softening at ~10-20 TeV) appears to have an approximately 'universal' rigidity-dependent shape common to protons, helium and other primary nuclei, per Lipari2019, though the slope values differ between species - a universality that holds for the FEATURE shape even while the underlying source slopes differ.

Schroer2021 documents the iron anomaly: AMS-02 Fe is anomalously hard at R < ~100 GV and its Fe/O ratio is in tension with the standard transport model AND with HEAO/ACE-CRIS/Voyager data, a discrepancy (~30-40% near 1 GeV/n) that the authors cannot resolve and suspect may be experimental.

A single set of Galactic transport parameters (diffusion + advection, with a high-rigidity break in the diffusion coefficient) consistently fits intermediate and heavy nuclei (Ne, Mg, Si, S up to Fe except the iron low-rigidity anomaly) per Schroer2021, supporting the propagation-break interpretation for most species.

Semi-analytical propagation tools like USINE (Maurin2019) are the machinery used to fit this picture - solving the diffusion/advection transport equation for Z=1-30 nuclei with force-field solar modulation - and USINE was used to hint at the high-rigidity break in the diffusion coefficient from AMS-02 B/C data, the same propagation break invoked to explain the hardening.

Dembinski2017's data-driven global spline fit deliberately avoids assuming power-law-plus-cutoff component shapes and instead cross-calibrates experiment energy scales across 10 GeV to 10^11 GeV, showing the all-particle and per-element structure (the ~5 TeV dip, the knee at ~3 PeV) emerges from a world-average once energy scales are reconciled rather than from one source/propagation model.
rationale: Read in full: all five papers. Nugget 1 = Adriani2011 (gamma_p ~2.820, gamma_He ~2.732, Delta-gamma=0.101). Nugget 2 = Schroer2021 section IV.C/Conclusions (three slopes: proton ~0.05 softer, He ~0.02 harder; at odds with DSA). Nugget 3 = Lipari2019 section 4 (universal rigidity-dependent shape across species even if slopes differ). Nugget 4 = Schroer2021 abstract/IV.B (iron hard R<100 GV, Fe/O tension with model and HEAO/ACE-CRIS/Voyager, ~30-40% at 1 GeV/n, possibly experimental). Nugget 5 = Schroer2021 section III-IV (single transport set fits Ne/Mg/Si/S/Fe except iron). Nugget 6 = Maurin2019 (USINE Z=1-30, force-field, hints high-rigidity diffusion break from AMS-02 B/C). Nugget 7 = Dembinski2017 (GSF no power-law assumption; energy-scale cross-calibration; 5 TeV dip, 3 PeV knee emerge from world-average). Maurin2019/Dembinski2017 context (tool + framework) not direct adjudicators of species universality.

intent: I'm building a heliospheric cosmic-ray modulation code and trying to decide whether to solve Parker's transport equation with stochastic differential equations (pseudo-particle/Markov solvers) or with a finite-difference grid scheme like ADI. I want to understand the concrete numerical trade-offs each group reports (stability, parallelism/cost, what part of phase space you get a solution at, dimensionality limits), and crucially whether groups fitting the SAME modern proton/helium spectra (PAMELA, AMS-02) with these different numerics end up recovering consistent diffusion-coefficient behavior and rigidity dependence. Pull from both the SDE-solver methodology papers and the application papers that fit spacecraft data.
nuggets: Parker's equation is traditionally solved by finite-difference schemes such as the Alternating Direction Implicit (ADI) method, whereas the SDE/pseudo-particle approach is the increasingly popular alternative (Dunzlaff2015; Corti2018; Song2021).

SDEs are unconditionally (numerically) stable while finite-difference/ADI schemes can become unstable for too-large time steps, and time-dependent 3D ADI is numerically unsuitable/unstable so that one spatial dimension must be sacrificed or the SDE approach adopted (Dunzlaff2015; Corti2018; Song2021).

An SDE/pseudo-particle solver computes the solution only at the phase-space point(s) of interest (a spectrum at Earth) and is embarrassingly parallel with independent trajectories, whereas a finite-difference solver computes f over the whole grid; the time-backward SDE formulation is the efficient choice for spectra at a point (Dunzlaff2015).

Corti2018 uses a 3D steady-state finite-difference (ADI) solver and, because a single model run is slow, fits AMS-02 monthly proton fluxes by generating a multi-million-model parameter grid (~3 million models, ~10 weeks, 4.6 TB) and interpolating, rather than a per-flux least-squares minimization (Corti2018 section 3).

Song2021 solves the SAME class of PAMELA/AMS-02 proton+helium spectra (2006-2017) with a time-dependent 3D SDE solver but searches the drift/diffusion parameter space with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC, Metropolis-Hastings), achieving best-fit normalized chi^2 mostly < 1 (Song2021).

Multiple groups, despite different numerics, agree that the parallel diffusion coefficient magnitude (normalization K_0 and a double-power-law rigidity dependence with K_perp ~= 0.02 K_parallel) is anticorrelated with solar activity and must vary in time to reproduce the spectra (Song2021; Wang2019; Ngobeni2020; Corti2018).

There is a documented partial DISAGREEMENT in the inferred rigidity dependence: Song2021 (SDE+MCMC best-fit) finds the parallel-MFP rigidity slope can be STEEPER at low rigidity than high rigidity during moderate/minimum activity, contrary to the steepening-at-high-rigidity reported by steady-state ADI-style models, and Song2021 explicitly attributes such differences partly to steady-state-vs-time-dependent and ADI-vs-SDE numerics (Song2021 section 4.3).

Wang2019 solves Parker's equation with the SolarProp SDE Monte-Carlo code in 2D time-dependent form, fitting Voyager-1 + PAMELA to derive the LIS, and finds an empirical power-law DC ~ <B_E>^-n with n ~= 2 between the diffusion coefficient and the near-Earth HMF (Wang2019).
rationale: Read in full: Dunzlaff2015, Song2021, Wang2019; Corti2018 and Ngobeni2020 read through methods+results. Zhao2013a: ABSTRACT-ONLY - the on-disk extract is a MISMATCHED paper (DOI 10.1002/jgra.50235, an observation-based heavy-nuclei model that does not solve Parker's equation), so grounded only on the get_paper abstract and used as low-weight context. Nugget 1 = Dunzlaff2015 section 2 ('traditionally solved using finite-difference'), Corti2018/Song2021 echo ADI. Nugget 2 = Dunzlaff2015 2.2 (SDE unconditionally stable, FD not), Corti2018 (time-dependence makes ADI unsuitable), Song2021 (time-backward SDE unconditional stability). Nugget 3 = Dunzlaff2015 (solution at one phase-space point, independent trajectories, highly parallel). Nugget 4 = Corti2018 section 3 (3 million models, ten weeks, 4.6 TB, interpolated). Nugget 5 = Song2021 abstract/3 (Metropolis-Hastings MCMC, chi^2/dof < 1). Nugget 6 = Song2021 4.1 (K_0 increasing to 23-24 minimum), Eq.10 (K_perp=0.02 K_parallel); Ngobeni2020 2.1 two-power-law; Corti2018 2.2; Wang2019 4.4 (k_0 vs HMF). Nugget 7 = Song2021 4.3 (rigidity-slope difference; attributed to steady-state-vs-time-dependent and ADI-vs-SDE). Nugget 8 = Wang2019 (SolarProp SDE; DC ~ <B_E>^-2). DATA-INTEGRITY FLAG: Zhao2013a on-disk extract is a wrong/mismatched paper; re-ingest recommended; excluded from gold_keys.

intent: Across the modulation groups that reproduce the proton-to-helium ratio from PAMELA and AMS-02, I want to know whether the physical conclusion - that the time/rigidity behavior of p/He below a few GV is driven by the mass-to-charge ratio A/Z and by the different proton vs helium local interstellar spectra rather than by species-dependent diffusion - is robust to the numerical solver used (3D steady-state finite-difference ADI vs 3D/2D SDE pseudo-particle, with parameters set by grid-scan vs MCMC vs manual tuning). I also want the shared modeling assumption that the same diffusion/drift coefficients (same mean free paths in rigidity) apply to protons and helium, and where the groups note residual quantitative discrepancies.
nuggets: It is a shared assumption across these models that protons and helium share the SAME diffusion/drift coefficients (the same mean free paths as a function of rigidity), so one parameter set reproduces both species' spectra simultaneously (Ngobeni2020; Corti2018; Song2021).

Corti2018, using a 3D steady-state finite-difference ADI solver, concludes the dependence of the diffusion tensor on the particle mass-to-charge ratio A/Z is the MAIN cause of the time dependence of p/He below ~3 GV (Corti2018 abstract).

Ngobeni2020, using a 3D drift (finite-difference, steady-state) model fitting PAMELA p and He 2006-2009, concludes the p/He differences arise from the combined effect of A/Z and especially the DIFFERENT proton vs helium VLIS slopes, with p/He above ~3-4 GV settling near ~5.5 essentially independent of modulation conditions and thus revealing the VLIS shapes (Ngobeni2020).

Ngobeni2020 explicitly shows all mean free paths and the drift scale are independent of A/Z (A/Z enters only through beta = v/c in the rigidity-to-energy conversion), so there is no fundamental species-difference in modulation at a given rigidity - the p/He time/rigidity structure comes from beta(A/Z) and the VLIS (Ngobeni2020 section 2.1).

Song2021 (3D time-dependent SDE + MCMC) reproduces the long-term time dependence of the AMS-02/PAMELA p/He but finds the simulated ratio systematically LOWER than observed, attributing the residual to underestimation of the proton flux / the assumed proton LIS - a quantitative discrepancy that the steady-state groups also flag as LIS-sensitivity (Song2021 section 4.2).

All four groups specify the modulation boundary at the heliopause/termination shock (Song2021 heliopause 120 au; Corti2018 termination shock 80 au, heliopause 122 au; Ngobeni2020 heliopause 122 au; Wang2019 termination shock 100 au) where the LIS/VLIS is imposed as the boundary condition, and all use a Parker/Smith-Bieber-type HMF with K_perp ~= 0.02 K_parallel.

Wang2019 (2D time-dependent SolarProp SDE) shares modulation parameters across CR species (p, He, B, C) in the same period and derives their LIS by fitting Voyager-1 + PAMELA/BESS/ACE, reinforcing the cross-group view that one diffusion parameterization serves multiple nuclei and that the LIS is the key species-distinguishing input (Wang2019).
rationale: Read in full: Song2021, Wang2019; Corti2018 read methods+fit, Ngobeni2020 read methods+results incl. 3.3 p/He. Dunzlaff2015 and Zhao2013a OFF (methods/Markov papers without p/He A/Z study). Nugget 1 = Ngobeni2020 3.2 (same parameters, only A/Z and VLIS differ), Corti2018 abstract (same mean free paths), Song2021 4.2 (one parameter set for both). Nugget 2 = Corti2018 abstract (A/Z main cause of p/He time dependence below 3 GV). Nugget 3 = Ngobeni2020 abstract/3.3 (p/He ~5.5 above ~4 GV, VLIS-revealing). Nugget 4 = Ngobeni2020 2.1 (MFPs independent of A/Z; beta depends on A/Z). Nugget 5 = Song2021 4.2 (ratio systematically low, proton-flux/LIS underestimation). Nugget 6 = boundary positions Song2021 2.2 / Corti2018 3 / Ngobeni2020 2.1 / Wang2019 3; K_perp=0.02 K_parallel each. Nugget 7 = Wang2019 5 (shared params across species; LIS from Voyager-1 + PAMELA). Distribution spans 4 papers: A/Z+VLIS conclusion in two FD steady-state models tested under SDE+MCMC, with Wang2019 corroborating.
